This time differs from 2021 because policymakers are no longer recovering from emergency shock interventions, but are instead managing high-interest-rate valuation pressures where macroprudential vulnerabilities are actively exposed by credit penalties. This elevates the probability of deploying the CCyB above 0% to build loss-absorbing capital against structural debt and asset valuation strains.

These regulatory bodies historically experience friction when aligning macroprudential policy changes due to differing institutional mandates and lengthy interagency rulemaking processes. However, when systemic risk warnings accumulate—such as vulnerabilities highlighted across asset classes and banking sector profits amid bond market turbulence—the historical frequency with which interagency friction entirely blocks macroprudential adjustments is relatively low. Once regulatory momentum is initiated by the Board of Governors, administrative friction and procedural hurdles rarely prevent the final implementation of capital buffer adjustments, as the structural mechanisms for rule finalization and voting are well-established and routinely overcome similar bureaucratic delays.
